title: How Border Patrol Is Helping Local Cops Expand Surveillance in California
author: Pascal Sabino
content:
People in California’s Central Coast are being tracked by an ever expanding
network of license plate reading cameras funded by federal immigration
dollars, even as misgivings over both surveillance and the Trump
administration’s deportation agenda have boiled over into full-blown protests.

In 2019, privacy advocates in California started [sounding the
alarm](https://www.aclunorcal.org/docs/Pages%20from%20DOCS_031319_1822.pdf)
after discovering that the San Luis Obispo County Sheriff’s Office had given
federal immigration officials access to data collected by the county’s
surveillance network, which at the time consisted of just one license plate
camera. Yet the sheriff’s network of automatic license-plate readers (ALPRs)
has since quietly multiplied with the help of funding from the federal
Department of Homeland Security aimed at forging more coordination between
local police and Border Patrol.

Purchasing records obtained by _Bolts_ show how San Luis Obispo County Sheriff
Ian Parkinson, who has held the office since 2011, has used money from a
little-known DHS program called Operation Stonegarden to grow his surveillance
network. First in 2019, not long after coming under fire for sharing data with
ICE, the sheriff tapped Stonegarden funds to expand his department’s network
of Motorola Vigilant license plate readers.

And then last year, according to budget documents, the sheriff allocated
$45,000 from the Stonegarden grant to pay for more ALPRs, just weeks before
the department set up a new network of 23 cameras from Flock, the nation’s
largest license plate reader company, which would cost the county $69,000
annually. A spokesperson for the San Luis Obispo County Sheriff told _Bolts_
that the Stonegarden funds the county board approved last year were not spent
on the expansion of the county’s Flock system, but would instead go to more
Motorola ALPRs.

The federal money seems to have made it easier for the sheriff to expand this
surveillance network without much oversight or scrutiny of the technology from
other local officials. Bruce Gibson, who sits on the governing board for San
Luis Obispo County, says there was no discussion of the surveillance cameras
or potential concerns about the technology last year when the board approved
using the Stonegarden grant to pay for license plate cameras as part of the
annual budget process. Gibson told _Bolts_ that the board typically defers to
the sheriff to select the department’s contractors, especially when they are
not paid by the county’s general funds.

Gibson said the series of scandals involving Flock and the “heinous and cruel
way” the federal government has used ALPR surveillance to carry out the
president’s [deportation dragnet](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/2026/aug/03/california-ice-immigration-raid) have made him more aware of
the potential for the technology to be abused.

“It didn’t enter my consciousness that there might be some significant policy
issues until the misuse of Flock became much more obvious,” Gibson told
_Bolts_.

Waves of reporting in recent years [have uncovered
that](https://www.404media.co/ice-taps-into-nationwide-ai-enabled-camera-
network-data-shows/) Flock cameras and other surveillance tech are being used
as a backdoor for local police to track immigrants for the federal government,
even in states like California and
[Washington](https://jsis.washington.edu/humanrights/publication/9480/), where
that kind of data-sharing is banned.

_Bolts_ ’ new investigation shows that this is no coincidence—the technology's
growth is fueled by funds meant to help enforce immigration laws in the first
place.

Records obtained by _Bolts_ via public information requests uncovered similar
findings as in San Luis Obispo across the state of California.

Despite the state’s strict restrictions on collaboration with federal
immigration authorities, and its broader reputation as a stalwart against the
Trump administration’s aggressive immigration agenda, many local law
enforcement agencies have funded their expansion of license plate reading
surveillance cameras with funding from this federal program specifically aimed
at increasing local collaboration with border enforcement: During the most
recent grant period, starting in 2024, departments across California received
at least $760,000 in Stonegarden grants to purchase license plate cameras,
often from Flock.

Surveillance companies directly reached out to some law enforcement agencies,
including the Imperial County Sheriff’s Office, to encourage them to apply for
these immigration funds and use them to purchase their cameras, records show.

In San Luis Obispo County, the money helped the sheriff's office grow its
network of cameras even during a recent wave of local activism against such
surveillance, as well as growing awareness of data
[breaches](https://www.wired.com/story/hackers-flock-camera-data-shows-how-
system-works/) across the country tied to Flock. Beyond sharing data on
immigrants, officers in other jurisdictions have used the company’s
surveillance network to stalk romantic partners in [at least 85
instances,](https://ij.org/the-ij-database-of-alpr-abuse) and also to [track
protesters](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/11/how-cops-are-using-flock-
safetys-alpr-network-surveil-protesters-and-activists) and [people obtaining
abortion care](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/10/flock-safety-and-texas-
sheriff-claimed-license-plate-search-was-missing-person-it).

Students at California Polytechnic State University, an anchor of the Central
Coast region, protested this year over the school contracting with Flock to
mount 17 cameras around campus. The students collected over 1,500 signatures
for a petition calling on the school to end its Flock contract, prompting the
student government to [unanimously demand](https://mustangnews.net/asi-board-
votes-flock-cameras/) that administrators take down the cameras.

And this July, nearby in the small community of Oceano, public officials
[rejected a request by the San Luis Obispo County
Sheriff](https://www.sanluisobispo.com/news/local/article316445401.html)’s
Office to install a Flock camera at a station run by the local utilities
commission. Clara Fulks, a privacy advocate in San Luis Obispo who has fought
against the cameras, says the community rejected the sheriff’s request because
“people just don't want to feel like they're being watched all the time.”

“It was a rare opportunity to actually vote on this,” Fulks told _Bolts_.
“Usually, it's not up to a vote.”

But privacy advocates say the infusion of money from federal partnerships like
Stonegarden has allowed local police to get around this sort of public
pressure to deploy and scale up invasive surveillance technologies without the
usual oversight. According to Gibson, the county board did vote to appropriate
Stonegarden funds to the sheriff for ALPRs, but there was no meaningful
discussion around the sheriff’s surveillance program since the item was
[buried in the
budget](https://www.slocounty.ca.gov/departments/administrative-office/forms-
documents/budget-documents/prior-years-county-special-district-
budgets/fy-2025-26-county-special-districts-
budgets#docaccess-f1a78569dee616e19f5e1ce436af2000) that county supervisors
approved last year.

“There really wasn't any discussion,” Gibson said.

Fulks says “people would be up in arms” if the San Luis Obispo sheriff’s
expansion of his ALPR network had been publicly discussed at county board
meetings. Even the residents who are not tuned in to the privacy risks
associated with mass surveillance would likely still balk at the use of border
and immigration funding to grow the network because “people are really aware
of the issues facing immigrants and ICE being in our jail,” Fulks told _Bolts.
_

Last year, the county voted on a separate pot of federal dollars, the State
Homeland Security Program, a grant meant to help police prevent terrorism that
the sheriff had previously used to fund license-plate readers. Even though
that program does not directly involve immigration enforcement, [community
members voiced concerns](https://www.newtimesslo.com/locals-concerned-
homeland-security-funding-for-slo-county-sheriff-could-aid-ice-17029956/) that
the money would still incentivize the sheriff to assist with deportations.

“Why would they allocate this money and allow it to be spent on surveillance
technology unless the federal agencies that are in these partnerships would
benefit from it?” Fulks said.

* * *

California departments are already banned from sharing license plate reader
data with agencies outside the state because of a privacy law adopted in 2015.
Under that law, police in the state must log each time they search the
cameras, and cities and counties are required to [give the public an
opportunity to give feedback on the
technology](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/media/2023-dle-06.pdf) before
first deploying license plate cameras.

But that privacy protection law is riddled with loopholes. Sheriffs have to
solicit public input before launching a surveillance program but need not
follow that public feedback, and they don’t need approval from a city council
or county board. In San Luis Obispo, Gibson said he thought the sheriff did
not have to participate in a public discussion of Flock before contracting
with the company in 2025 since the county already ran a license plate reader
program for years, even if it used a different vendor.

Despite the guardrails in state law, there are documented examples of privacy
violations where officers who are authorized to use local ALPRs have searched
the network on behalf of someone who wasn’t supposed to have access, or have
informally passed along private data. Investigations [by
CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2025/06/california-
police-sharing-license-plate-reader-data/) and [Oakland
Privacy](https://oaklandprivacy.org/dozens-of-california-law-enforcement-
agencies-illegally-sharing-license-plate-reader-data/) over the past two years
have uncovered search logs showing local officers across the state using the
cameras to assist federal immigration officials, including officers at the
Riverside County Sheriff’s Office, Los Angeles Police Department and the San
Diego County Sheriff’s Office.

The San Luis Obispo County Sheriff’s Office has blocked the release of logs
that document how the license plate cameras are being used, claiming those
logs are exempt from public disclosure in response to public records requests
filed by _Bolts_.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sought to enforce the ban on out-of-
state sharing at least once, when he sued the city of El Cajon last year for
sharing data gathered by ALPRs with federal immigration authorities and more
than two dozen other states. But there have been no consequences for many
other instances of police violating these data-sharing restrictions in recent
years in places like [San Diego
County](https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2025/06/california-police-
sharing-license-plate-reader-data/), [Elk
Grove,](https://www.cbsnews.com/sacramento/news/audit-who-is-accessing-elk-
grove-license-plate-camera-data/) [Newport
Beach](https://oaklandprivacy.org/dozens-of-california-law-enforcement-
agencies-illegally-sharing-license-plate-reader-data/) and [Los
Angeles](https://lapublicpress.org/2025/06/lapd-is-illegally-sharing-license-
plate-data-with-ice-and-border-patrol/).

It has largely been advocacy groups, rather than the attorney general, who
have gone after departments for illegally sharing data with federal
immigration agencies. The ACLU of Northern California [sued the Marin County
sheriff in 2021](https://www.aclunorcal.org/press-releases/marin-county-
sheriffs-office-shared-automated-license-plate-reader-information-with-
outside-law-enforcement-agencies/) to stop the data sharing, and San Diego
advocates represented by the local ACLU affiliate [sued the city of San Diego
and the San Diego Police Department in September](https://www.aclu-
sdic.org/press-releases/aclu-foundation-of-san-diego-imperial-counties-sues-
the-city-of-san-diego-and-san-diego-police-department-to-end-unconstitutional-
alpr-mass-surveillance-program/) alleging violations of privacy protections
and seeking to remove all license plate cameras from the city. Organizers
seeking stronger guardrails around police technology have warned that existing
regulations like the 2015 privacy law hadn’t accounted for the explosion in AI
capabilities that make Flock’s network so powerful.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Bolts-
Surv-1-flattened-2400x1800.jpg)Illustration by Daniel Zender for Bolts

In recent years, advocates have pushed for surveillance protections that
include a stronger enforcement mechanism. Last year, lawmakers in both of
California’s legislative chambers passed regulations for automatic license
plate readers that would have established annual random audits to make sure
departments are not illegally sharing sensitive data, but Governor Gavin
Newsom [vetoed the bill](https://www.gov.ca.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2025/10/SB-274-Veto.pdf), saying tighter rules could impede
investigations and warning that the state hadn’t budgeted for such auditing.

Flock’s key selling point is that its subscribers can track drivers using not
only their own cameras, but also those installed by other Flock customers
across the company’s sprawling surveillance network. In a proposal the company
made to the San Luis Obispo County Sheriff’s Office, obtained under an open
records request, Flock touted how other nearby agencies are also part of its
network, including the Santa Barbara County Sheriff’s Office with 25 cameras
and the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office with 102.

The agreements local agencies enter into for Stonegarden funds specify that
the program is meant to enhance intelligence sharing with Border Patrol by
requiring participants to join bi-monthly meetings and provide activity
reports to their federal partners. The version of the Stonegarden agreement
signed by California agencies contains a provision specifically declaring that
the partnership complies with state’s sanctuary protections that forbid local
officers from assisting with immigration enforcement, and instead pertains to
wider border security issues.

Some advocates say these Stonegarden agreements shouldn’t even be allowed in
California due to the immigrant protections enacted in 2018 known as the
California Values Act, or Senate Bill 54, which restricts local police from
cooperating with federal immigration enforcement. There are still carveouts
and exceptions in the law that give local police and sheriffs some discretion
to maintain federal partnerships. The California Values Act also explicitly
bans officers from working under the supervision of federal agents, and
federal oversight is a key component of Stonegarden; still, the ban applies
only when the operation’s primary purpose is immigration enforcement.

Tony Cipolla, spokesperson for the San Luis Obispo County Sheriff’s Office,
told _Bolts_ that the agency’s participation in Operation Stonegarden is
mostly focused on coordinating with state and federal law enforcement “to
jointly enhance security along the U.S. land and water borders,” noting that
the county “has had a history for maritime narcotics smuggling.”

A spokesperson for the state agency that administers Homeland Security grants
for California counties and tribal governments told _Bolts_ that Stonegarden
funds “aren’t used for immigration enforcement,” but instead support Border
Patrol operations “to enhance border security and improve coordination on
illegal drug seizures and anti-terrorism efforts.” The AG’s office has said
[it cannot determine](https://calmatters.org/education/2026/02/uc-san-diego-
homeland-security-border-patrol/) whether Stonegarden grants comply with the
law, while advocates argue that they don’t.

“Operation Stonegarden goes directly against the protections that California
has established,” Frederick Carroll, legal director for the ACLU of San Diego
& Imperial Counties, told _Bolts_.

In San Diego County, the state’s largest recipient of Stonegarden funds,
advocates have long warned there’s a hidden price for such free money from the
feds.

“If they say, ‘We’re going to give this to you for free,’ then there doesn't
have to be that public debate, and there doesn't have to be a public,
transparent conversation about what's the purpose of this technology,” said
Homayra Yusufi, senior policy strategist for the Partnership for the
Advancement of New Americans and a privacy advocate with the Transparent and
Responsible Use of Surveillance Technology coalition in San Diego.

“Does it actually make us safer? Is it effective? Who else has access to that
information?” Yusufi told _Bolts_. “These are conversations that every
locality should have when they're going to be potentially getting technology
that's this powerful, and that impacts everyone's rights in this way. But that
conversation is cut all together when they're just grant funded.”

Brian Hofer, executive director of Secure Justice, an organization that works
to curb police surveillance in California, contends that when local police owe
their equipment to a partnership with federal immigration authorities, they
may feel obligated to share more information.

“There’s always going to be some sort of expectation, and it’s usually data
sharing,” Hofer told _Bolts._ “They (the feds) give us equipment, so there is
a financial incentive for the local police department to keep those central
guys happy, which is often by cooperating and providing data, so that they can
keep getting funding. It absolutely incentivizes that kind of relationship.”

* * *

Carroll with the ACLU called the Stonegarden program a kind of slush fund for
quietly installing powerful police surveillance equipment and technology
that’s incredibly hard for communities to dismantle once they become aware of
it.

“These are toys that were initially intended to face outward—never to be
turned on Americans,” Carroll said. “But what has happened is that
increasingly, federal money is going towards corporations to monitor human
beings, and it is being carried out against local rules and regulations and
against the fundamental principles of what it means to live in this country.”

Participation in [the $85 million Operation Stonegarden
program](https://grantedai.com/grants/homeland-security-grant-program-hsgp-
operation-stonegarden-opsg-federal-emergency-management-agency-fema-999ff9a3)
is pretty common, but it has largely flown under the radar. In California,
only three counties are listed as grant recipients on the federal award list
for the most recent granting period, but those participating sheriffs then
pass much of that money to dozens of other police agencies across the state.
For instance, the police department for the University of California San Diego
[received](https://calmatters.org/education/2026/02/uc-san-diego-homeland-
security-border-patrol/) a sub grant from the county sheriff’s office, which
this year became [highly contentious among
students](https://calmatters.org/education/2026/07/uc-san-diego-homeland-
security-border-patrol-students-protest/) who argued it was inappropriate for
campus officers to work closely alongside border patrol.

In some instances, counties have cut ties with Operation Stonegarden due to
the concerns around working with federal agents. In Arizona, the Pima County
Board of Supervisors voted to stop taking the federal money in 2018 after
activists warned that local officers would be roped into doing immigration
enforcement and risk incidents of racial profiling. In Santa Cruz County, also
in Arizona, [Sheriff David Hathaway pulled out of Operation
Stonegarden](https://www.kjzz.org/fronteras-desk/2025-01-30/santa-cruz-county-
sheriff-pulls-out-of-federal-stonegarden-program-for-cbp-collaboration) last
year out of concern that officers are expected to prioritize the orders of
their federal partners over local interests if they accept the money.

Gibson, the San Luis Obispo County supervisor, says he’s grown nervous by how
the technology has advanced in recent years from a more rudimentary network of
cameras to a sprawling dragnet surveillance tool enabled by artificial
intelligence. Flock cameras are known for being able to identify cars using
bumper stickers or dents and able to track people across most of the country.
Footage gathered by the cameras and stored has been used to track not just
where people have gone but also to [algorithmically
predict](https://cdt.org/insights/ai-in-policing-automatic-license-plate-
readers/) where they will go next based on their prior movements.

“The technology gets its foot in the door with a simple use case that you can
accept. And then as the technology evolves and gets more sophisticated, and
more connected, and more powerful, there are consequences that come from that
evolution,” Gibson told _Bolts_. “I think that's very much what's happened
with these cameras.”

The growing privacy concerns in San Luis Obispo around the sheriff’s expanding
surveillance network dovetail with local advocates’ criticism of his
willingness to help immigration agents. California’s immigrant protections
allow jails to turn people over to ICE if they have certain prior convictions,
though it was done only once by the San Luis Obispo County Sheriff’s Office in
2024. But since President Donald Trump resumed his crusade of mass
deportations the following year, Parkinson’s office has handed at least 107
people into ICE custody, the department’s records show. The jail has since
become a regular site for protests against ICE.

Fulks, the local privacy advocate, suspects that community anger over the
sheriff’s cooperation with ICE would have led to scrutiny of a Border Patrol-
funded surveillance network, had county officials publicly discussed the
Stonegarden agreement.

She says any assurance that the sheriff’s surveillance network isn’t assisting
Border Patrol rings hollow considering it was purchased with funds meant for
that purpose.

“They're trying to say our data is not shared with federal agencies,” Fulks
told _Bolts_. “But if our county is purchasing cameras with money from the
federal government that is specifically for the purpose of connecting and
strengthening relationships between county sheriff departments and federal
agencies—then that would tell me that there is an intention to share this data
as well with federal agencies.”
